newsitem.title: USA: Anti-tobacco forces suffer two losses in Senate.
newsitem.headline: Anti-tobacco forces suffer two losses in Senate.

text.p: Anti-tobacco forces suffered two losses in the Senate on Wednesday, failing in a bid to fund an initiative against teenage smoking and in an attempt to scrap a crop insurance programme for tobacco farmers.
Both measures, offered as amendments to a larger farm spending bill, were narrowly defeated on procedural grounds.

Involving only $34 million apiece, a small sum by federal standards, the measures might not have attracted much attention in other years. But they take on added symbolism as Congress and the White House begin to consider a proposed $368 billion settlement of tobacco litigation between the industry and 40 states suing them.
"Once again, the tobacco companies have prevailed," said Sen. Tom Harkin, an Iowa Democrat who sponsored the youth smoking plan.

"Tobacco is not like any other crop in America. Tobacco is the only crop grown in America with a body count," said Sen. Richard Durbin, a Democrat of Illinois who co-sponsored the crop plan with Republican Sen. Judd Gregg of New Hampshire.
Critics said the measures were unfair to tobacco farmers.
"Tobacco is something that everybody wants to chew at, but what we forget about is the farmer," said Sen. Wendell Ford, a Democrat from tobacco-producing Kentucky.

The Clinton Administration had requested $34 million for the Food and Drug Administration to start enforcing its new rules against teenage smoking. FDA officials have said that amount would not have been enough for nationwide enforcement.

States already have laws on the books forbidding minors to buy cigarettes but they are poorly enforced. New U.S. rules require stores to check IDs before selling cigarettes or smokeless tobacco to anyone who looks under age 27.

The Senate Appropriations Committee, however, cut the funds to less than $5 million, and the House panel cut it to $24 million. Tobacco foes in the House are expected to try to add funds when the farm spending bill reaches the floor.

In committee, Appropriations Chairman Sen. Ted Stevens, an Alaska Republican, argued that the funds were unnecessary because the settlement proposal would pay for anti-smoking efforts. However, it is far from certain that the settlement will swiftly be enacted into law.
On the floor debate, Stevens argued against the Harkin measure on technical grounds, saying it used a revenue raising device that is not allowed in a spending bill.
The second measure would have halted the $34 million programme that subsidises insurance for tobacco farmers in case their crops fail or are struck by a disaster.
Durbin said fewer than 70 crops get these insurance subsidies, and hundreds do not. He said a crop that has "no benefit to human health" should not be among the covered ones.

Also Wednesday, Durbin and other tobacco foes said they would introduce a bill to prevent U.S. promotion of tobacco exports and required more explicit health warning labels on cigarette exports. The proposed tobacco settlement encompasses many changes in the way cigarettes are marketed in the United States but does not address the thriving overseas market.
"We don't want a settlement agreement with a loophole big enough for the Marlboro Man to ride Joe Camel through," said one of the sponsors, Representative Lloyd Doggett, a Texas Democrat.
